editorial_review.black_atlantic: Coordinator reviewed all nodes and relationships; independently checked Wintz nursing review abstract, Hartman’s Du Bois criticism and Fuentes’s named Hartman inspiration. Joint-publication date/coeditor metadata added separately.
editorial_review.micro_intellectual: Coordinator and independent reviewer checked all five nodes and 12 endpoint repairs; peer independently read GHI Pocock/Koselleck exchange and Dahlstrom review. Ginzburg original Italian collection and English translation date/track corrected before acceptance.

scope: A bounded first expansion, not completion of all130 proposed biographies or systematic coverage of the named historiographical traditions. No identity/citation merges, automatic reading bridges, new field taxonomy or changed group-review years. Existing archive and source qualifications preserved; the earlier publisher witness has an explicit edition-review addendum. OpenAlex stays paused. User authorized push after Astra review and corrections; publication verification pending.

entries.label: Romila Thapar
entries.reading_limits: Read on 2026-10-24: the Library of Congress assessment; Thapar’s 2015 speech; her 2014 publisher excerpt at pp. 21–24; the displayed opening extracts of Talbot’s 2014 and Veluthat’s 2004 reviews. Books are unread; the 1961 and 1984 titles are catalogue-only. The 2015 speech is not the similarly titled 2014 essay collection. Later work and reception have not been surveyed; no career ending is asserted.

entries.label: Cheikh Anta Diop
entries.reading_limits: Read on 2026-10-24: Tine’s introduction, section 2 and conclusion in an author-authorized repository; the publisher’s search-rendered account; BnF/INHA metadata; UCAD’s centenary programme metadata. Diop’s books and Dieng’s original critiques are unread. Claims from 1981 and 1989 are mediated through Tine. No verdict on the population of ancient Egypt is established by publisher praise or a commemorative programme. Tine’s death-year error is excluded; UCAD gives 1986. Original French titles and later translations are not conflated.

entries.label: Liang Qichao
entries.reading_limits: Read on 2026-10-24: authorized Columbia translations of selected writings; Dirlik’s introduction and epilogue passages; Blitstein pp. 180–182; Zheng’s relevant historical discussion. The 1902 and 1920 works are known through named academic readers, not newly read in Chinese. The 1921 milestone dates lectures, without conflating them with later editions of Chinese historical research methods. Blitstein’s 2021 issue date is distinct from 2020 online/copyright metadata. No direct relation to individual European thinkers is inferred from resemblance.

entries.label: Gu Jiegang
entries.reading_limits: Read on 2026-10-24: Richter’s complete 1982 obituary and the opening/references of her separate China Quarterly article; PKU biography; Lu’s Chinese/English abstracts; Jenco’s publisher abstract; Kim’s English abstract; Zheng’s Gu discussion; Dirlik’s selected epilogue passages. Gu’s original works remain unread. Chinese intellectual and philological traditions are not treated as mere imports of European methods. The 1926 series start is supported by Richter’s references; her obituary’s 1927 date is retained here as a source discrepancy, not silently harmonized. Jenco’s and Kim’s divergent interpretations remain attributed.

entries.label: Ibn Khaldun
entries.reading_limits: Read on 2026-10-24: selected pages of Princeton’s translated author-text excerpt; Simon pp. 64–65 and 99–103; Stanford section 15; Hannoum’s selected sections. The Arabic originals and the larger history/autobiography themselves are unread; their writing chronology is mediated through Simon. Three separate writing milestones are shown, without turning modern translations into original contributions or assigning an invented single publication date. The 1405 point marks the final dated autobiographical material, not a confidently dated completion. Modern field comparisons do not establish direct intellectual descent, and this entry does not stand for all Islamic historiography.

entries.label: Masao Maruyama
entries.reading_limits: Read on 2026-10-24: Nakajima’s selected chapter pages and Lim’s English abstract; NDL catalogue metadata. The original Japanese essays and 1986 commentary remain unread, known through named readers. The prior source’s narrower primary-opening review is retained, including its caution about the platform’s 1989 reissue description. The 1952 collection, 1974 translation and 1940–44 essays are distinct. Existing person ID and intellectual-history roster wording are preserved.

entries.label: W. E. B. Du Bois
entries.reading_limits: Read in part: the 1896 preface and chapter I opening, and the 1903 Forethought and chapter I, in public-domain transcriptions. The 1899 and 1935 books are known here through the named readings by Anderson and Williams. Their conclusions are attributed to them. Hartman’s criticism comes from her 2020 interview, not a newly read passage of Wayward Lives. Period racial/evolutionary vocabulary is historical evidence, not endorsed terminology. Later activism and writings are not comprehensively surveyed. Existing edge_241 retains its Du Bois/Gilroy diaspora-resource claim; no duplicate personal Atlantic arrow is added.

entries.label: Carter G. Woodson
entries.reading_limits: Own words read: the 1919 education preface/opening, the 1918 migration preface/opening and the 1933 preface/chapter I in transcriptions. Original/edition dates remain distinct. Pyne’s Library of Congress essay and the NPS supply mediated institutional history, community support and public statements. Pyne contrasts Woodson’s account of obstructive fundraising with Meier/Rudwick’s and Winston’s readings; those underlying studies were not independently read here. Most book chapters and the complete journal remain unread. Public-history placement describes a specific educational practice, not later professional membership.

entries.label: Darlene Clark Hine
entries.reading_limits: The 1989 Signs article was read at pp.912–916 and 919–920 in an institutional copy; Hine’s qualifications on economic motives and her own conceptual difficulties are retained. The nursing book is mediated by Wintz’s repository abstract; the review PDF was inaccessible. The 2003 contribution is read only in its publisher-indexed opening extract. No full-book or full-address reading, complete career survey or new original-date claim for Hine Sight is made. Institutional bibliographies/reissues give inconsistent dates for Hine Sight; that chronology is left for separate edition research.

entries.label: Saidiya Hartman
entries.reading_limits: Read on 24 October 2026: “Venus in Two Acts,” pp.7–14, in a public institutional copy; the Jean interview in full; selected Bulley interview answers on archives, Lose Your Mother and waywardness. The three books remain unread beyond these descriptions and retrospective accounts. Acknowledged narrative failure and limits of speculation are part of the method. The Du Bois critique is her 2020 statement, not an independently read book passage. Existing roster notes and their earlier unread qualifications remain as historical reading records; the new sources state this later scope. Existing edges_1213 and _1215 retain the aggregate archive/Atlantic and archive/Black-history interpretations.

entries.label: Marisa J. Fuentes
entries.reading_limits: Read: Rutgers’s author abstract for the 2010 article; the publisher-authorized 2017 book excerpt; Davenport’s interview in full; the 2017 AAIHS roundtable essay in full; and the Rutgers Press description, contents and collaborative credits for Scarlet and Black. Full books, the 2010 article body and the complete joint issue remain unread. The interview’s unnamed scholarly objections are her report. The new entry retains the existing people record’s unresolved external-identity qualification; no Wikidata identity is invented. Later publications listed by Rutgers are not silently treated as read arguments. Existing archive-to-Atlantic and archive-to-Black-history edges stay unchanged.

entries.label: Carlo Ginzburg
entries.reading_limits: The 1976 book remains unread as a whole; its date and Menocchio context retain the earlier reviewed publisher record. New reading on 2026-10-24: selected Clues pp. 96–101 through the university-hosted scan/OCR; 1993 Microhistory pp. 22–24, 26–30, 32–34 reread. Original Italian, full Clues essay and cited Freud/Morelli works were not collated. The 1986 Italian collection and its 1989 English translation are dated separately from the earlier component essays; the 1989 translation is on the editions track, not an original-contribution milestone. The 1993 retrospective explicitly denies that Kracauer’s work founded his microhistorical practice; retrospective affinity is not transmitted influence. The existing qualified group-endpoint claims about Ginzburg are reattached to this individual entry with their IDs and evidence intact. No life dates, complete career interval or review-through year are asserted.

entries.label: Giovanni Levi
entries.reading_limits: Existing readings and their translation limits remain. Reread on 2026-10-24: complete ten-page Portuguese Geertzism translation (1999), especially pp. 142–146; original Italian uncollated. The earlier complete official OCR reading of the 1989 biography essay is retained, with its opening reread in Persée; OCR quotations were not newly reproduced. Inheriting Power remains known through bibliography and Ginzburg’s named account, not a new whole-book reading. The 2019 contribution is read in the publisher-rendered opening and notes only, after direct access failed; the limited argument about global histories is attributed accordingly. Geertz’s and Darnton’s books were not independently re-read. Older person-specific critiques retain their original edge IDs and qualifications.

entries.label: Quentin Skinner
entries.reading_limits: No complete career review or whole-book reading. Prior source qualifications remain. Fresh 2026-10-24 reading: 1969 article pp. 37–38 and 50–52; 2002 manuscript answers 1 and 6; Liberty before Liberalism preface ix–xiv and printed pp. 1–4, with the publisher copyright leaf distinguishing first publication 1998 from lecture 1997 and Canto reissue 2012; Pocock’s published 1996 criticism at pp. 54–55. The original Collingwood passage remains uncollated. Skinner’s retrospective recollection is explicit reception evidence, not a shared method of every Cambridge historian. Collective edges that also name Dunn, Pocock or Brett stay on the group entry; only claims specifically about Skinner move to his individual endpoint.

entries.label: J. G. A. Pocock
entries.reading_limits: Fresh reading 2026-10-24: printed pp. 3–4, 9–11 in the 2009 publisher excerpt of the 1962 methodological inquiry; the complete 1996 concepts-and-discourses contribution pp. 47–58; Robertson’s 2025 article pp. 1–4 closely, with later sections/endnotes consulted for the six-volume sequence. The earlier reading of The Machiavellian Moment introduction vii–x is preserved, not represented as a newly read complete book. No body of the 1957 or 1999–2015 books was read. Pocock explicitly cannot read German and discusses the Geschichtliche Grundbegriffe through Richter; the new objections preserve that limit and his praise of complementary inquiry. His private correspondence and late political essays were not read. The 1996 publication is separate from the December 1992 symposium.

entries.label: Reinhart Koselleck
entries.reading_limits: The retained Futures Past source records the exact earlier selected chapter/preface readings and their limits. Fresh 2026-10-24 reading: chapter 5 pp. 85 and 91–92, with the surrounding analytical distinctions; the 1996 reply pp. 59–66 closely, plus its concluding context; the complete six-page Dahlstrom review of Olsen. Original German texts, lexicon articles and the full 1959/1967/2000 books were not read. The lexicon’s 1972 date is bibliographic metadata; its methodological account rests separately on the primary reply and existing primary passages. Nietzsche’s quotation and Weber’s typology are specific resources, not total genealogies. New prose paraphrases rather than reproduces source quotations. The early-book reception is a reader’s report of another reader, with no new direct claim about Habermas’s uncollated review.
